title: A stale Projects config, a gate with no way out, and a test suite that lied about why it failed
lede: One day, three unrelated problems. The Kitsune card was already written into the Projects tab's code, but a config file saved before that card existed would never pick it up on a live deployment. Separately, reviewing the live gate the way a recruiter actually would turned up a screen with no escape hatch — nothing, not even the CV, reachable without typing a company name. And re-reading the test suite cold turned up two of its own bugs: one that silently leaked state into later tests, and one that turned a single stuck process into 28 confusing failures instead of one clear message. Below is what I found, what I changed, and how I checked each one.
meta: Code review + UI review + local server
Verified with: 4 new unit tests, the full 48-test suite, a direct fault-injection check, a manual Chrome walkthrough on both localhost and the live site
tiles: a skip link that needed no company name
Real bugs fixed in the tests
a state leak and a fragile startup check
Bugs found on the live site
config, images, console and network all came back clean

findings.title: A deployed site can silently miss a brand-new default project card
findings.trigger: Comparing the Kitsune card in app/config_store.py's DEFAULT_CONFIG against what load_config() actually returns for a config.json saved earlier
findings.before: load_config() only fills in settings keys that are completely missing; "projects_cards" already existed on disk, so the newer default card never got added, and nobody would notice from the code alone
findings.after: load_config() adds any default card not yet offered, tracked per repo, and leaves the list alone afterwards — including if the owner later removes a card on purpose
findings.cause: DEFAULT_CONFIG gained the Kitsune card after some sites had already saved their own projects_cards list, and a plain setdefault() never merges list contents, only missing keys
findings.fix: The first version of this fix tracked one global "has this run" flag. That broke the moment a third default card (the churn project, below) was added after the flag was already set on the live site — the flag being true skipped the check entirely, so the new card was silently never offered. Switched to tracking which repos have been offered individually, so a card added to DEFAULT_CONFIG later still gets its own first chance, independent of earlier ones.

findings.title: The homepage would keep growing with every new project
findings.trigger: Thinking ahead to adding more project cards over time
findings.before: The Projects section rendered every card in the list, one under another, straight on the homepage
findings.after: The homepage shows the first two cards with an always-visible "All projects" link below them (it reads "View all N projects" once there are more than two); every card, always, lives at its own /projects page
findings.cause: The Projects grid had no cap — it was built when there was only one project card
findings.fix: Added a FEATURED_PROJECTS cutoff in shell.js, a new /projects page, and pulled card rendering into one shared project-card.js module so the homepage preview and the full list can never draw a card differently

findings.title: A recruiter who didn't want to play along could never reach the CV
findings.trigger: Walking through the site cold, the way a recruiter skimming 200 applications would
findings.before: The only way past the gate was typing a company name and waiting through the boot animation — nothing, not even the CV download, was reachable before that
findings.after: A quiet "Skip to the CV" link next to the existing report link submits an empty visitor name through the same /api/gate path the form already used, landing straight on the dashboard with Download Full CV visible
findings.cause: The gate was designed around the chatbot persona first and the plain-CV path was never added as a fallback
findings.fix: Refactored the form's submit handler into a shared enterWith() function and called it from both the form and the new skip link, so the skip path gets identical session handling, error handling and boot sequence — no second code path to drift out of sync. Restyled both gate links as a small pill pair instead of plain underlined text.

findings.title: One test silently poisoned every test that ran after it
findings.trigger: Re-reading tests/test_app.py cold, checking every test that mutates shared state for a matching restore
findings.before: test_config_put_validation set the site title to a throwaway value and never restored it — no try/finally, unlike test_maintenance_mode right next to it, which does restore its state
findings.after: The mutation and all its assertions are now wrapped in try/finally, so the real title is restored even if an assertion in between fails
findings.cause: The test was written by copying the request/assert pattern from elsewhere in the file, but not the teardown pattern
findings.fix: Wrapped the body in try/finally, matching the pattern test_maintenance_mode already used a few tests earlier in the same file

findings.title: A stuck process produced 28 confusing failures instead of one clear one
findings.trigger: This is the exact failure I hit in an earlier debugging session: a day-old orphaned server was still holding the test suite's port, and the whole suite failed with opaque connection errors
findings.before: The startup loop retried for 10 seconds and then silently fell through with no assertion — every test afterward failed with its own ConnectionError, none of them pointing at the real cause
findings.after: The loop now raises one clear RuntimeError naming the port and suggesting a `lsof` check if the server never comes up
findings.cause: The loop was written to retry, but nobody added the "and if it never works, say so clearly" case
findings.fix: Added a flag set only on a successful request inside the loop, and one explicit raise after it if that flag was never set — proved it by occupying the port on purpose and confirming the new message fires instead of the old pile of ConnectionErrors

strengths.title: The card data and GitHub merge were never the problem
strengths.body: Once a card is actually in the list, the GitHub-data merge, the cover image, the stats and the styling all worked correctly on the first try, on both the homepage and the /projects page.

strengths.title: The responsive CSS and the self-test page held up under a second, cold look
strengths.body: Re-checking the CSS without the context of having written it, the mobile breakpoint, touch-target sizing and prefers-reduced-motion handling all still held up fine.

strengths.title: The live site matched the local one
strengths.body: Network inspection of the live site showed every request — including both project cover images — returning 200. An earlier screenshot that looked like broken images was a timing artifact of screenshotting before the images decoded, not a real bug.

checks.name: New migration unit tests (4)
checks.detail: stale config backfills the missing card; the backfill persists and runs once; a later deliberate removal is not undone; a fresh config already has every default card

checks.name: Homepage and /projects, manual check in Chrome
checks.detail: homepage shows exactly the 2 featured cards, /projects lists every card, identical styling, working back link, no console errors

checks.name: Gate skip link, manual check in Chrome
checks.detail: lands on the dashboard with no company typed; Download Full CV is visible immediately

checks.name: Full unit test suite (48 tests)
checks.detail: clean run, no failures; 23 failures seen in an earlier back-to-back run were a stuck process holding the test port, not a regression — see the fault-injection check below

checks.name: Fault-injection check: test port pre-occupied on purpose
checks.detail: produces exactly one RuntimeError naming the port, instead of the pile of opaque ConnectionErrors this failure mode used to cause

checks.name: Live site, manual check
checks.detail: console clean, all network requests 200 including both project images

also: Shared the card-rendering code between the homepage and /projects in one project-card.js module, so the two can't quietly drift apart.
Documented the homepage cutoff and the /projects page in the README's project-management section.
First version only linked to /projects once there were more than two cards — with exactly two, the page had no way in from the UI at all. Made the link always visible.
Added the customer segmentation & churn prediction project as a third card — the first real test of the homepage cutoff and the backfill fix above.
Read tests/test_app.py cold, the way someone unfamiliar with it would, checking every state-mutating test for a matching teardown — that's what caught the state leak above.
method: Read through app/config_store.py's load_config() and compared it against what a config.json saved before the Kitsune card existed would actually return.
Wrote the migration plus four unit tests against a temporary DATA_DIR, isolated from the real site's data.
Reviewed the live gate flow as a recruiter would experience it, cold, before looking at any code.
Re-read the test file cold, checking every state-mutating test for a matching restore, the same discipline test_maintenance_mode already followed.

Fixed the config bug, the homepage cap, the gate, the state leak, and the fragile startup check; wrote a fault-injection check that occupies the test server's port on purpose, to prove the new error path actually fires rather than just assuming it would.

Ran the full suite clean, then re-ran it with the port blocked to confirm both the before and after behaviour, then started a local server and checked every page in Chrome including the browser console.
Checked the live production site's network requests and console directly rather than trusting a screenshot that looked wrong.
Committed each fix separately, then pushed to main.
